CALIFORNIA LABOR CODE SECTION 925 — FORUM SELECTION AND CHOICE-OF-LAW RESTRICTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Corp.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California Labor Code Section 925, which restricts certain forum-selection and choice-of-law provisions that Acme Corp. may require of Jordan Lee as a condition of employment. It states the statute's own terms. It does not evaluate whether any specific provision in any specific agreement between Acme Corp. and Jordan Lee is subject to, or violates, Section 925, and it does not determine whether any such provision is void, whether an exception applies, or what either party should do about any particular agreement.

CORE PROHIBITION: OUT-OF-STATE ADJUDICATION AND LOSS OF CALIFORNIA-LAW PROTECTION
California Labor Code Section 925(a) prohibits an employer from requiring an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would do either of two things: (1) require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California, or (2) deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California. Section 925(d) defines "adjudication" for purposes of this section to include both litigation and arbitration, so the prohibition is not limited to court-forum clauses -- it also reaches a clause requiring arbitration outside California, or an arbitration clause that would apply another state's substantive law to a controversy arising in California.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) An employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would do either of the following: (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California. (2) Deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 925(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 925, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=925.)
  "(d) For purposes of this section, adjudication includes litigation and arbitration."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 925(d) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 925, subd. (d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=925.)
  Known gap: Both citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code Section 925(a) and 925(d)), not independent corroborating sources. This clause covers only the prohibition itself and the statute's own definition of "adjudication"; it does not cover the voidability consequence, the individually-negotiated-with-counsel exception, the attorney's-fee provision, or the applicability date, each addressed in this document's other clauses. The statute's own text does not define "primarily resides and works in California" or "a claim arising in California" beyond that phrasing, and this clause does not determine whether a specific employee or a specific claim meets either description. No case law is cited in this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

VOIDABILITY AND THE GOVERNING-LAW CONSEQUENCE OF VOIDING
California Labor Code Section 925(b) states that a contract provision violating subdivision (a) is voidable by the employee, not automatically void. If the employee requests that such a provision be voided and it is rendered void at that request, the statute's own text further provides that the matter shall then be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(b) Any provision of a contract that violates subdivision (a) is voidable by the employee, and if a provision is rendered void at the request of the employee, the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 925(b) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 925, subd. (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=925.)
  Known gap: This clause covers Section 925(b) only. Because the statute makes a violating provision voidable rather than void, the statute's own text does not itself describe how or in what forum an employee exercises the option to void a provision (for example, by objection in a pending proceeding, by a separate action, or otherwise); that procedural mechanism is not addressed by this clause. This clause does not address what happens to any part of a contract or provision the employee does not seek to void, or to the remainder of the agreement generally. No case law is cited in this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

COURT'S AUTHORITY: INJUNCTIVE RELIEF AND ATTORNEY'S FEES
California Labor Code Section 925(c) states that, in addition to injunctive relief and any other remedies available, a court may award an employee who is enforcing their rights under this section reasonable attorney's fees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(c) In addition to injunctive relief and any other remedies available, a court may award an employee who is enforcing his or her rights under this section reasonable attorney’s fees."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 925(c) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 925, subd. (c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=925.)
  Known gap: This clause covers Section 925(c) only. The statute's own text uses the word "may," so a fee award under this subdivision is discretionary with the court, not automatic upon a successful enforcement action. The statute's own text authorizes an award of the employee's reasonable attorney's fees; it does not, in this subdivision, use or define the phrase "actual costs," and this clause does not state that costs (as distinct from attorney's fees) are separately authorized by this subdivision. The phrase "any other remedies available" is not itself defined or enumerated in this subdivision, and this clause does not identify what those other remedies are. This subdivision does not address a fee award running the other direction, to an employer, and this clause does not state that one is or is not available. No case law is cited in this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

EXCEPTION FOR A CONTRACT INDIVIDUALLY NEGOTIATED WITH THE EMPLOYEE REPRESENTED BY COUNSEL
California Labor Code Section 925(e) states that the section does not apply to a contract with an employee who is in fact individually represented by legal counsel in negotiating the terms of an agreement to designate either the venue or forum in which a controversy arising from the employment contract may be adjudicated, or the choice of law to be applied.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(e) This section shall not apply to a contract with an employee who is in fact individually represented by legal counsel in negotiating the terms of an agreement to designate either the venue or forum in which a controversy arising from the employment contract may be adjudicated or the choice of law to be applied."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 925(e) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 925, subd. (e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=925.)
  Known gap: This clause covers Section 925(e) only. The statute's own text conditions the exception on the employee being "in fact individually represented by legal counsel in negotiating the terms" of the venue, forum, or choice-of-law provision specifically; this clause does not define what representation or negotiation is sufficient to satisfy that standard, and whether a particular employee's representation meets it is a fact-specific question this clause does not resolve. This subdivision, by its own terms, removes the protection of the entire section for a qualifying contract; this clause does not address whether the exception can apply to only part of an agreement. No case law is cited in this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

APPLICABILITY DATE
California Labor Code Section 925(f) states that the section applies to a contract entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017. The statute's own enactment note on the California Legislative Information website confirms that Section 925 was added by Statutes 2016, Chapter 632, Section 1 (SB 1241), effective January 1, 2017.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(f) This section shall apply to a contract entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 925(f) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 925, subd. (f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=925.)
  "(Added by Stats. 2016, Ch. 632, Sec. 1. (SB 1241) Effective January 1, 2017.)"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 925, enactment history note (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 925, history note (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=925.)
  Known gap: The two citations below are drawn from the same statutory section as published on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov -- subdivision (f)'s applicability text and the page's own enactment/history note for the section -- not from two independent sources. This clause states only the applicability trigger and the enactment date; it does not determine, for any specific contract, whether that contract was entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017, and it does not address how a contract's modification or extension is identified for this purpose, which the statute's own text does not define. No case law is cited in this clause; it rests on the statutory text and the source page's own history note.

SIGNATURE
Executed at Sacramento, California on September 4, 2026.

Acme Corp.

By: _________________________

Jordan Lee

Signature: _________________________
